tagline: Separate boulevards became a parkway along a vanished lake’s shoreline.
intro: Skyline Parkway follows the former shoreline of Glacial Lake Duluth for 28 miles across Duluth, from Becks Road to Seven Bridges Road. Overlooks along the road take in Lake Superior and the St. Louis River Bay. Explore Minnesota presents this scenic byway as a view over the harbor and Lake Superior’s shoreline, with neighboring parks and trails extending the trip beyond the road.

William K. Rogers, Duluth’s first park board president, conceived the road in 1888. Construction began the following April, and traffic used it by August; rock and difficult terrain slowed its westward growth. In 1894, the Duluth park board voted unanimously to name the earlier boulevard for Rogers. Meanwhile, Samuel F. Snively began a separate scenic road along Amity Creek in 1899. Maintenance difficulties led him to seek park board help, and the board took control in 1910. In 1929, a newspaper competition gave the combined boulevard system its Skyline Parkway name.

Starting at Becks Road, the western section reaches Stewart Creek and Bardon’s Peak before Thompson Hill. Enger Tower rises near the parkway farther across Duluth. Toward the northern end, Hawk Ridge offers a vantage for spring and fall migration; the route ends at Seven Bridges Road.

moments.title: Stewart Creek Bridge
moments.text: Dark green gabbro gives Stewart Creek Bridge its color and its pointed profile: double sawtooth rows of stone top the railings. Built around 1925 for Skyline Parkway, the bridge carries a single arch across a deep ravine. Its high supports and curving form belong to the Picturesque design tradition of the mid-19th century. The walls beside the arch continue back to retain the road approaches, while pointed boulders line the approach itself. Duluth rehabilitated the bridge in 2012–2013. The locally quarried stone spans 30 feet, with the arch rising 10 feet above its springing point.

moments.title: Enger Tower
moments.text: Enger Tower’s five stone stories rise 80 feet above Enger Hill, with windows on each level reached by stairs. The tower honors Bert Enger, a Norwegian immigrant who found success selling furniture in Duluth and left the city part of his estate, including Enger Hill. Crown Prince Olav and Crown Princess Märtha of Norway dedicated it in 1939. After a 2011 renovation, their son King Harald V and Queen Sonja came for its rededication. The view reaches across the Twin Ports. Former balcony entrances are barred; the balconies themselves were removed after falling into disrepair.

moments.title: Hawk Ridge
moments.text: Lake Superior redirects the migration at Hawk Ridge. Birds of prey coming south from Canada follow the shore rather than cross the lake, funneling between the coastline and the bluffs before crossing the ridge. The same concentration once attracted hunters. The Duluth Bird Club secured enforcement of the city’s ban on discharging firearms here. P. B. Hofslund and the club began annual counts in 1951; banding began in 1972. The ridge is now a nature reserve and bird observatory. In 1972, the city bought 135 acres at the highest part of the ridge.
